newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean currency hits record low.
newsitem.headline: South Korean currency hits record low.

text.p: The South Korean won slumped to a new record low against the dollar on Wednesday as dealers bet the government wanted a weaker currency to boost exports and cut a mounting current account deficit.
"The financial authorities, pressured by a snowballing current account deficit, are taking a backseat to the rising dollar," said Lee Chang-seon, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute.
"Narrowing the current account deficit is a pressing issue for the government. It has no other means to slash the deficit but to bet on exports by letting the won drop," he said.
A weak won makes South Korean products more competitive by trimming export prices.
The won fell to an all time low of 843.00 on Wednesday before traders said the central Bank of Korea intervened in the afternoon. The bank gave a routine denial when asked if it stepped in.

"The central bank intervened temporarily to slow the dollar's rise but not to stop it," said a dealer at a Seoul-based European bank. "The dollar could have risen over 850 today if not for the intervention."
Traders said the won has weakened considerably this week on heavy import settlements and delays in global depositary receipt plans by banks.
Plans by Korea Long-Term Credit Bank and Boram Bank to issue a combined $270 million worth of global depositary receipts abroad have been delayed until next year due to the ailing Seoul stock market.
Although the won's depreciation prompted worries of a rise in inflation, economists said the government feels more at ease in handling inflation.
"The government thinks it's more important to squeeze the current account deficit," said Lee of LG. "They feel they can somehow manage to curb consumer prices."

Han Sang-chun, economist at Daewoo Economic Research Institute, said: "A ballooning current account deficit is an embarrassment for Kim Young-sam's administration facing a presidential election next year."
